items.stem: Electric current is
options: the force on a moving charge
the opposition to the flow of charge
the rate of flow of charge
items.answer: the rate of flow of charge
items.markingKey: I = Q/t: current is charge passing a point per second.

items.stem: A phone charger supplies a small circuit board. The current is tripled while the time stays the same. Predict, with a reason, how the charge that flows changes.
items.markingKey: Using Q = It: charge that flows ∝ current; factor = 3.00 = 3.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: In a school experiment, a resistor is connected to a variable power supply. The time is tripled while the current stays the same. Explain how the charge that flows changes.
items.markingKey: Using Q = It: charge that flows ∝ time; factor = 3.00 = 3.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A current of 3.00 A flows for 120 s. Calculate the charge that flows.
A current of 1.50 A flows through a heater element for 2 minutes. Calculate the charge that passes.
items.markingKey: t = 2 × 60 = 120 s; Q = It = 1.50 × 120 = 180 C. Forgetting to convert minutes is the usual error.

items.stem: A current of 0.250 A flows through a heater element for 2 minutes. Calculate the charge that passes.
items.markingKey: t = 2 × 60 = 120 s; Q = It = 0.250 × 120 = 30.0 C. Forgetting to convert minutes is the usual error.

items.stem: A small motor connected to a 3 V supply takes a current of 1.50 A while running for 600 s. (a) Calculate the power of the device. (b) Explain what is meant by the e.m.f. of the battery.
items.answer: (a) 4.50 W (b) The energy transferred by the battery per unit charge moved around the complete circuit.

items.stem: A 6 V battery drives a current of 0.200 A through a lamp for 600 s. (a) Calculate the charge that passes through the device. (b) Calculate the power of the device.
How is an ammeter connected in a circuit?
options: It is not connected, it is held near the wire
items.markingKey: An ammeter measures the current through a component so it is placed in series; it has very low resistance.

items.stem: In a metal wire, the charges that move to form a current are
items.markingKey: Metals conduct because of free (delocalised) electrons.

items.stem: An engineer tests a car headlamp circuit. The current is doubled while the time stays the same. Explain how the charge that flows changes.
items.markingKey: Using Q = It: charge that flows ∝ current; factor = 2.00 = 2.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: Explain why the current is the same at all points in a series circuit.
items.answer: Charge is not used up; the same charge passes each point every second because there is only one path.

items.stem: A charge of 240 C passes a point in 120 s. Calculate the current.
A current of 0.250 A flows through a heater element for 15 minutes. Calculate the charge that passes.
items.markingKey: t = 15 × 60 = 900 s; Q = It = 0.250 × 900 = 225 C. Forgetting to convert minutes is the usual error.

items.stem: In a torch, the battery has an e.m.f. of 9 V and the bulb draws 1.50 A. It is switched on for 30 s. (a) Calculate the energy transferred by the battery. (b) Explain what is meant by the e.m.f. of the battery.
items.answer: (a) 405 J (b) The energy transferred by the battery per unit charge moved around the complete circuit.

items.stem: A voltmeter is connected
options: in series with the cell only
between the ammeter and the cell
items.markingKey: Voltmeters measure the p.d. across a component and have very high resistance.

items.stem: 3 cells, each of e.m.f. 1.2 V, are connected in series in a torch, but one is put in the wrong way round. Explain the total e.m.f.
items.answer: 1.20 V: the reversed cell cancels the e.m.f. of one correctly placed cell, so total = (3 − 2) × 1.2 V.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: e.m.f.s in series add with direction; 1 mark: correct value.

items.stem: 3 cells, each of e.m.f. 2.0 V, are connected in series in a torch, but one is put in the wrong way round. Explain the total e.m.f.
items.answer: 2.00 V: the reversed cell cancels the e.m.f. of one correctly placed cell, so total = (3 − 2) × 2.0 V.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: e.m.f.s in series add with direction; 1 mark: correct value.

items.stem: A 1.50 V battery moves 40 C of charge around a circuit. Calculate the energy it transfers.
A 1.50 V battery moves 2 C of charge around a circuit. Calculate the energy it transfers.

In a torch, the battery has an e.m.f. of 12 V and the bulb draws 1.20 A. It is switched on for 60 s. (a) Calculate the energy transferred by the battery. (b) Calculate the resistance of the device when working.
2 cells, each of e.m.f. 1.5 V, are connected in series in a torch, but one is put in the wrong way round. Explain the total e.m.f.
items.answer: 0 V: the reversed cell cancels the e.m.f. of one correctly placed cell, so total = (2 − 2) × 1.5 V.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: e.m.f.s in series add with direction; 1 mark: correct value.

items.stem: A student investigates a heating element connected to a power supply. The p.d. is reduced to one third while the charge stays the same. State and explain how the energy transferred changes.
items.answer: The energy transferred becomes one third.
items.markingKey: Using W = QV: energy transferred ∝ p.d.; factor = 0.333 = 0.333. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A source transfers 270 J of energy when 60 C of charge passes through it. Calculate its e.m.f.
A 3 V battery drives a current of 1.20 A through a lamp for 120 s. (a) Calculate the charge that passes through the device. (b) Explain what is meant by the e.m.f. of the battery.
items.answer: (a) 144 C (b) The energy transferred by the battery per unit charge moved around the complete circuit.

items.stem: In a torch, the battery has an e.m.f. of 3 V and the bulb draws 0.400 A. It is switched on for 600 s. (a) Calculate the power of the device. (b) Calculate the number of electrons passing in 600 s (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C).
What is the unit of resistance?
Explain, using ideas about electrons, why a thinner wire has more resistance than a thicker wire of the same material and length.
items.answer: A thinner wire has fewer free electrons per unit length available to carry current / a narrower path, so a given p.d. drives a smaller current.

items.stem: Sketch-describe the I–V graph of a semiconductor diode and explain its use.
items.answer: Almost zero current in reverse and below about 0.6–0.7 V forward; current rises steeply above that. It lets current flow in one direction only (rectification).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: graph shape; 1 mark: one-way conduction.

items.stem: A current of 0.300 A passes through a 20 Ω resistor. Calculate the potential difference across it.
A potential difference of 0.500 V is applied across a 2 Ω resistor. Calculate the current.
A 10 kΩ resistor carries a current of 0.300 mA. Calculate the p.d. across it.
items.markingKey: V = IR = 0.300 × 10⁻³ A × 10 × 10³ Ω = 3.00 V. Prefixes kΩ and mA cancel.

items.stem: In a practical, Tariq measures the p.d. across different lengths of constantan wire while keeping the current at 0.4 A. Results (length/cm, p.d./V): 20, 0.12; 40, 0.24; 60, 0.36; 80, 0.48; 100, 0.6. (a) Calculate the resistance for each length. (b) Describe the relationship. (c) State one source of error and how to reduce it.
items.answer: (a) R = V/I: 0.300 Ω, 0.600 Ω, 0.900 Ω, 1.20 Ω, 1.50 Ω. (b) R is directly proportional to length (doubling L doubles R). (c) Wire heating changes R: switch off between readings / use small current; or contact position uncertainty: use crocodile clips at marked positions.
items.markingKey: (a) 2 marks; (b) 1 mark proportional; (c) 1 mark error + 1 mark improvement.

items.stem: In a practical, Ana measures the p.d. across different lengths of constantan wire while keeping the current at 0.5 A. Results (length/cm, p.d./V): 20, 0.08; 40, 0.16; 60, 0.24; 80, 0.32; 100, 0.4. (a) Calculate the resistance for each length. (b) Describe the relationship. (c) State one source of error and how to reduce it.
items.answer: (a) R = V/I: 0.160 Ω, 0.320 Ω, 0.480 Ω, 0.640 Ω, 0.800 Ω. (b) R is directly proportional to length (doubling L doubles R). (c) Wire heating changes R: switch off between readings / use small current; or contact position uncertainty: use crocodile clips at marked positions.
items.markingKey: (a) 2 marks; (b) 1 mark proportional; (c) 1 mark error + 1 mark improvement.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Why does the resistance of a filament lamp increase as the current increases? (b) How does the resistance of a wire change if its cross-sectional area is doubled?
items.answer: (a) The filament gets hotter (b) It halves
items.markingKey: (a) Higher temperature → ions vibrate more → more collisions with electrons. (b) R ∝ 1/A.

items.stem: A student says, "Resistance is the gradient of the I–V graph." Explain the error.
items.answer: R = V/I. On an I–V graph (I on the y-axis) the gradient is I/V = 1/R, so a steeper line means a smaller resistance.

items.stem: A wire of constant temperature is used in a circuit. The length of the wire is halved while the cross-sectional area of the wire stays the same. Predict, with a reason, how the resistance of the wire changes.
items.answer: The resistance of the wire halves.
items.markingKey: Using R ∝ L/A: resistance of the wire ∝ length of the wire; factor = 0.500 = 0.500. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A constantan wire is tested in a practical. The cross-sectional area of the wire is multiplied by 4 while the length of the wire stays the same. Predict, with a reason, how the resistance of the wire changes.
items.answer: The resistance of the wire becomes a quarter.
items.markingKey: Using R ∝ L/A: resistance of the wire ∝ cross-sectional area of the wire^-1.00; factor = 4.00^-1.00 = 0.250. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: The p.d. across a lamp is 2.40 V and the current is 0.100 A. Calculate its resistance.
A wire has a resistance of 8 Ω. A second wire of the same metal is 0.500 times as long and has 2.00 times the cross-sectional area. Calculate the resistance of the second wire.
A 3 V battery drives a current of 0.200 A through a lamp for 600 s. (a) Calculate the charge that passes through the device. (b) Explain what is meant by the e.m.f. of the battery.
items.answer: (a) 120 C (b) The energy transferred by the battery per unit charge moved around the complete circuit.

items.stem: Which equation gives electrical power?
A phone charger supplies a small circuit board. The p.d. is reduced to a quarter while the current stays the same. Predict, with a reason, how the power changes.
items.markingKey: Using P = IV: power ∝ p.d.; factor = 0.250 = 0.250. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A torch bulb is connected to a battery pack. The current is multiplied by 5 while the p.d. stays the same. State and explain how the power changes.
items.markingKey: Using P = IV: power ∝ current; factor = 5.00 = 5.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A 2400 W appliance is connected to a 240 V supply. Calculate the current it draws.
An appliance draws 5.00 A from a 120 V supply. Calculate its power.
A 9.5 kW electric shower is used for 0.200 hours each day. Electricity costs $0.18 per kWh. Calculate the cost of using it for 7 days.

A 2900 W appliance runs from the 230 V mains for 10 minutes. (a) Calculate the current. (b) Choose a suitable fuse from 3 A, 5 A and 13 A and justify your choice. (c) Calculate the energy transferred in joules.
items.answer: (a) 12.6 A (b) 13 A – the smallest rating just above the normal current (c) 1.74 × 10⁶ J
items.markingKey: (a) I = P/V = 2900/230 = 12.6 A [2]; (b) 13 A, just above working current so it melts if a fault increases the current [2]; (c) E = Pt = 2900 × 600 = 1,740,000 J [2].

items.stem: A 1500 W metal-cased heater is connected to the 230 V mains with a three-pin plug. (a) Choose a fuse from 3 A, 5 A and 13 A and justify the choice. (b) Explain why the cable to the appliance must not be too thin. (c) State one advantage of a residual current circuit breaker over a fuse.
items.answer: (a) 13 A (b) A thin cable has more resistance and would overheat with this current, risking fire. (c) It acts faster and can be reset.

items.stem: What is a kilowatt-hour (kWh)?
options: The power of a 1 kW appliance
The current in a 1 kW appliance
The energy transferred by a 1 kW appliance in 1 hour
items.answer: The energy transferred by a 1 kW appliance in 1 hour

items.stem: A phone charger supplies a small circuit board. The current is multiplied by 5 while the p.d. stays the same. Predict, with a reason, how the power changes.
items.markingKey: Using P = IV: power ∝ current; factor = 5.00 = 5.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A household appliance is used each evening. The power of the appliance is reduced to one third while the time it is switched on stays the same. Predict, with a reason, how the energy transferred changes.
items.answer: The energy transferred becomes one third.
items.markingKey: Using E = Pt: energy transferred ∝ power of the appliance; factor = 0.333 = 0.333. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A 30.0 W appliance is connected to a 6 V supply. Calculate the current it draws.
A 2.0 kW heater is used for 3.50 hours each day. Electricity costs $0.15 per kWh. Calculate the cost of using it for 7 days.

In a torch, the battery has an e.m.f. of 6 V and the bulb draws 0.500 A. It is switched on for 300 s. (a) Calculate the energy transferred by the battery. (b) Explain what is meant by the e.m.f. of the battery.
items.answer: (a) 900 J (b) The energy transferred by the battery per unit charge moved around the complete circuit.

items.stem: Conventional current flows from
options: the negative terminal to the positive terminal
the positive terminal to the negative terminal
items.answer: the positive terminal to the negative terminal
items.markingKey: Conventional current: + to − around the external circuit; electrons flow the other way.

items.stem: Explain the difference between conventional current and electron flow.
items.answer: Conventional current flows from + to −; electrons actually move from − to + around the external circuit.

items.stem: A torch bulb is connected to a battery pack. The time is multiplied by 4 while the current stays the same. State and explain how the charge that flows changes.
items.answer: The charge that flows becomes 4 times bigger.
items.markingKey: Using Q = It: charge that flows ∝ time; factor = 4.00 = 4.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: How long does it take for 750 C of charge to pass when the current is 2.50 A?
A current of 4.00 A flows through a heater element for 5 minutes. Calculate the charge that passes.
items.markingKey: t = 5 × 60 = 300 s; Q = It = 4.00 × 300 = 1200 C. Forgetting to convert minutes is the usual error.

items.stem: A 12 V battery drives a current of 0.200 A through a lamp for 60 s. (a) Calculate the energy transferred by the battery. (b) Calculate the resistance of the device when working. (c) Calculate the number of electrons passing in 60 s (e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C).
The electromotive force (e.m.f.) of a source is
options: the charge stored in the source
the electrical work done by the source in moving a unit charge around a complete circuit
the current produced by the source
items.answer: the electrical work done by the source in moving a unit charge around a complete circuit
items.markingKey: e.m.f. = energy supplied per unit charge by the source (V = W/Q).

items.stem: A phone charger supplies a small circuit board. The p.d. is reduced to a quarter while the charge stays the same. Predict, with a reason, how the energy transferred changes.
items.answer: The energy transferred becomes a quarter.
items.markingKey: Using W = QV: energy transferred ∝ p.d.; factor = 0.250 = 0.250. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A 230 V battery moves 20 C of charge around a circuit. Calculate the energy it transfers.

A small motor connected to a 3 V supply takes a current of 1.20 A while running for 120 s. (a) Calculate the energy transferred by the battery. (b) Calculate the resistance of the device when working. (c) Explain what is meant by the e.m.f. of the battery.
items.answer: (a) 432 J (b) 2.50 Ω (c) The energy transferred by the battery per unit charge moved around the complete circuit.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) How does the resistance of a wire change if its cross-sectional area is doubled? (b) What is the unit of resistance?
items.markingKey: (a) R ∝ 1/A. (b) R = V/I, measured in ohms.

items.stem: A student investigates a heating element connected to a power supply. The resistance is reduced to one third while the p.d. stays the same. Explain how the current through the resistor changes.
items.answer: The current through the resistor triples.
items.markingKey: Using I = V/R: current through the resistor ∝ resistance^-1.00; factor = 0.333^-1.00 = 3.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A current of 0.250 A passes through a 2 Ω resistor. Calculate the potential difference across it.
The p.d. across a lamp is 15.0 V and the current is 0.750 A. Calculate its resistance.
A 12 V battery drives a current of 0.200 A through a lamp for 120 s. (a) Calculate the energy transferred by the battery. (b) Explain what is meant by the e.m.f. of the battery.
items.answer: (a) 288 J (b) The energy transferred by the battery per unit charge moved around the complete circuit.

items.stem: A shop runs its air conditioning every day. The power of the appliance is doubled while the time it is switched on stays the same. Explain how the energy transferred changes.
items.markingKey: Using E = Pt: energy transferred ∝ power of the appliance; factor = 2.00 = 2.00. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.markingKey: Using E = Pt: energy transferred ∝ power of the appliance; factor = 1.50 = 1.50. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.markingKey: (a) I = P/V = 2800/230 [2] (b) just above working current [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) How is an ammeter connected in a circuit? (b) Conventional current flows from
items.answer: (a) In series with the component (b) the positive terminal to the negative terminal
items.markingKey: (a) An ammeter measures the current through a component so it is placed in series; it has very low resistance. (b) Conventional current: + to − around the external circuit; electrons flow the other way.

items.stem: Explain why an ammeter must have a very low resistance.
items.answer: It is in series, so a large resistance would reduce the current it is measuring.

items.stem: Explain why a current of 2 A for 5 s moves the same charge as 1 A for 10 s.
A current of 0.200 A flows for 300 s. Calculate the charge that flows.
A current of 2.00 A flows through a heater element for 5 minutes. Calculate the charge that passes.

One volt is equal to one
Explain the difference between e.m.f. and potential difference.
items.answer: e.m.f. is the energy given per unit charge by a source; p.d. is the energy transferred per unit charge by a component.

items.answer: (a) a straight line through the origin (b) ohm (Ω)
items.markingKey: (a) Ohmic conductor: I ∝ V at constant temperature. (b) R = V/I, measured in ohms.

items.stem: Explain why the I–V graph for a filament lamp curves.
items.answer: As current rises the filament heats up, its resistance increases, so current rises less steeply.

items.stem: A potential difference of 10.0 V is applied across a 20 Ω resistor. Calculate the current.

In a practical, Ethan measures the p.d. across different lengths of constantan wire while keeping the current at 0.4 A. Results (length/cm, p.d./V): 20, 0.1; 40, 0.19; 60, 0.29; 80, 0.38; 100, 0.48. (a) Calculate the resistance for each length. (b) Describe the relationship. (c) State one source of error and how to reduce it.
items.answer: (a) R = V/I: 0.250 Ω, 0.475 Ω, 0.725 Ω, 0.950 Ω, 1.20 Ω. (b) R is directly proportional to length (doubling L doubles R). (c) Wire heating changes R: switch off between readings / use small current; or contact position uncertainty: use crocodile clips at marked positions.
items.markingKey: (a) 2 marks; (b) 1 mark proportional; (c) 1 mark error + 1 mark improvement.

items.stem: Explain why a 3 kW heater costs more to run for an hour than a 100 W lamp.
items.answer: Energy = power × time; the heater transfers 30 times as much energy each hour and you pay per kWh.

items.stem: Explain why the kilowatt-hour is used instead of the joule on electricity bills.
items.answer: A joule is tiny; household use is millions of joules, so kWh gives convenient numbers.

items.answer: The power dissipated in the resistor becomes one third.
items.markingKey: Using P = I²R: power dissipated in the resistor ∝ resistance; factor = 0.333 = 0.333. 1 mark relationship, 1 mark conclusion.

items.stem: A 12 V battery drives a current of 0.500 A through a lamp for 120 s. (a) Calculate the energy transferred by the battery. (b) Explain what is meant by the e.m.f. of the battery.
